questions.q: What is the correct syntax to create an index over only the rows where Status = 'Open'?
options: CREATE INDEX IX_Orders_Active ON dbo.Orders (CustomerId, OrderDate) WHERE Status = 'Open';
CREATE INDEX IX_Orders_Active ON dbo.Orders (CustomerId, OrderDate, Status);
CREATE FILTERED INDEX IX_Orders_Active ON dbo.Orders (CustomerId, OrderDate);
CREATE INDEX IX_Orders_Active ON dbo.Orders (CustomerId, OrderDate) HAVING Status = 'Open';
questions.explain: A filtered index adds a WHERE predicate directly to the CREATE INDEX statement, storing only rows matching that predicate.

questions.q: What is the classic use case for a filtered index, per this lesson?
options: A column where most rows share one uninteresting value (like NULL) and only a small minority hold the value queries actually care about
Indexing every column in a very wide table
Replacing the clustered index on a heap
Indexing a column that is never queried at all
questions.explain: Filtered indexes shine when a small, interesting subset of rows (e.g., non-NULL CancelledReason) would otherwise be buried among millions of uninteresting rows in a full-table index.

questions.q: Why is a filtered index on active rows typically smaller and faster than a full-table index on the same columns?
options: It stores only the rows matching its filter predicate, so it's smaller, cheaper to maintain, and more likely to fit in the buffer pool
SQL Server automatically compresses filtered indexes at a higher ratio than regular indexes
Filtered indexes are stored in memory only and never touch disk
Filtered indexes don't require an index key at all
questions.explain: Excluding the vast majority of uninteresting rows (e.g., archived orders) shrinks the index's footprint on disk and in the buffer pool.

questions.q: When can the query optimizer actually use a filtered index for a given query?
options: Only when it can prove, from the query's WHERE clause, that the query's results are a subset of the index's filter predicate
Always, regardless of the query's WHERE clause
Only when the query uses SELECT *
Only on clustered indexes
questions.explain: SQL Server must be able to guarantee at compile time that the query's filter is provably covered by the index's WHERE clause before it can use the filtered index.

questions.q: Why might a filtered index fail to be used when a stored procedure filters using a parameter like WHERE Status = @Status instead of a literal?
options: The optimizer often can't prove at compile time that @Status matches the index's filter predicate, since the parameter's value isn't known until runtime
Parameterized queries are always slower than literal queries regardless of indexing
Stored procedures cannot use any nonclustered indexes
Filtered indexes are automatically dropped whenever a parameter is used
questions.explain: Because the literal filter value isn't visible at compile time with a parameter, SQL Server often can't establish the provable-subset guarantee needed to use the filtered index.
